Weaker property market won't do much to ease inflation, according to one economist
The property market's fall isn't over yet, but the impact it will have on reducing inflation isn't enough.
That's according to economist Alan Oster, who spoke to business correspondent and presenter David Taylor on The Business last night.

"Brisbane is starting to fall, and Perth has just started, so I would say in Sydney, Melbourne, maybe another 1.5 to 2% fall," he says."And you basically get much bigger falls in the other capital cities where essentially the downturn has only just started."But generally, it's going to continue to fall at least to the end of this year."
"Brisbane is starting to fall, and Perth has just started, so I would say in Sydney, Melbourne, maybe another 1.5 to 2% fall," he says.
"And you basically get much bigger falls in the other capital cities where essentially the downturn has only just started.
"But generally, it's going to continue to fall at least to the end of this year."
One would think lower house prices would surely ease inflation pressures.
But Mr Oster thinks the impact won't be much.
"You've got things like high levels of government spending that keeps demand strong, you've got the impact of what's really happening globally," he says.

"So oil prices, I don't think are going to come down anytime soon."It's a combination of domestic prices and also international prices."So I don't think you will see anything other than at least a three in the core inflation to the end of the year."
"So oil prices, I don't think are going to come down anytime soon.
"It's a combination of domestic prices and also international prices.
"So I don't think you will see anything other than at least a three in the core inflation to the end of the year."
That basically means he thinks inflation data will be above 3%. For the RBA to be comfortable with inflation, and reduce the chance of another interest rate hike, inflation needs to sit between 2-3%.

Jobseekers exploited by recruitment scammers on LinkedIn
The ABC has observed an uptick in fraud targeting jobseekers as soon as they update their online status to indicate they are looking for work.
It includes fake job ads, fraudsters posing as recruiters with "cloned" profiles and people taking advantage of desperate jobseekers by offering to help with CV writing for significant sums of money.

Nasdaq Composite hits new record high
The Nasdaq surged to a fresh high on Monday, as earnings optimism and lower oil prices offset rising bond yields.
Nvidia and Microsoft boosted Wall Street's tech index as investors focused on a dip in oil prices and looked ahead to quarterly earnings reports.
It was the Nasdaq's second day of sharp gains after weaker-than-expected jobs data on Friday dampened expectations for an interest rate hike from the Federal Reserve at its policy meeting this month.

The biggest moves of the day were in Brazilian assets, which logged historic gains after right-wing candidate Flavio Bolsonaro's strong showing in the first round of voting in the presidential election suggested he is a strong favourite to win the second and decisive round in three weeks.
The Nasdaq Composite closed up +0.9% to 31,076 points.

Self-funded retirees spend up on culture and recreation
There wasn't a lot of good news in the Melbourne Institute of Applied Economic & Social Research's Monthly Inflation Gauge and Cost of Living report.
Essentially, it says inflation to September was running at 4.8% annually, a faster increase in the cost of prices than the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) figure of 4% to August.

(For a long time, the ABS only examined inflation on a quarterly basis in its Consumer Price Index (CPI) series. It updated it to monthly, like most similar stats bodies, but for a long time the Reserve Bank and institutions were open that they didn't think it was as "robust" as the once-every-three-months series.)
But the best thing in it is the category breakdown by age group and type.
Did you catch it?
Third row from the bottom, on the right-hand side.
The biggest single bump wasn't petrol, but recreation and culture costs for self-funded retirees.
Clearly someone was buying the expensive IMAX tickets to see The Odyssey …
